newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian edible oil trade seeks oilseeds imports.
newsitem.headline: Indian edible oil trade seeks oilseeds imports.

text.p: The Indian oilseeds trade on Wednesday welcomed the relaxation of storage controls but called on the government to end a ban on imports which it said are needed to put idle crushing capacity to use.

Last Friday, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram announced in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget that a law restricting use of storage facilities for oilseeds and edible oil would be invoked only in emergencies.
The act had prevented wholesale dealers in metropolitan cities from stocking more than 80 tonnes of edible oil and 200 tonnes of oilseeds.
Edible oil dealers said the restriction had hampered efficient trade and that its relaxation could be a step towards creating futures trading in the commodity.

"Our demand for the storage control act has been met, but our strong demand is for allowing oilseeds imports," K.M.L. Chabbra, executive director of the Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT), told Reuters.
"It is a step in the right direction as storage control is one of the barriers for futures trading," Navinbhai Shah, president of Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, told Reuters.
Industry officials urged the government to allow the import of oilseeds needed to meet idle refining capacity, which according to COOIT currently stands at about 60 percent.
"We strongly support import of oilseeds to activate the domestic idle refining capacity," G.K. Sood, chief executive of the Vanaspati Manufacturers Association of India, told Reuters.
Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said on Tuesday the government had received COOIT's demand for allowing oilseeds imports to generate additional employment opportunities.
Imports could be used to boost exports of extractions and would increase supplies of domestic edible oil, COOIT said.
"A final decision on the matter is yet to be taken," Yadav said.
Chabbra said COOIT will renew its plea for allowing oilseeds imports at its bi-annual convention, scheduled for the northern city of Agra on March 15 and 16.

Shah said edible oil importers had not signed any commitments in the past two weeks because of uncertainty over whether the government might increase the edible oil import duty to 30 percent from 20 percent.
But Chidambaram kept the duty unchanged in the budget.
"That fear has been dispelled but new (import) commitments will be booked for arrivals only after June as the domestic summer crop has started arriving," Shah said.

Yadav said India imported nearly 1.1 million tonnes of edible oil between April and December 1996. The U.S. Agriculture Department said on Tuesday that India was expected to import 1.3 million tonnes of edible oil in 1996/97.
Industry officials said domestic edible oil prices had eased by about 500 rupees ($14) per tonne in the past week because of plentiful summer crop arrivals.
They said groundnut oil was quoted at 34,000 rupees per tonne, soybean oil at 27,800, palm olein at 28,000 and sunflower oil (crude) at 25,000 rupees per tonne.
The government has forecast the 1996/97 (July-June) summer oilseeds crop at 9.7 million tonnes, unchanged from 1995/96.
